title: Not as others without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all things. Your line was pray without ceasing. What did you find to be thankful for inside a hard thing? Day five hundred ninety-four.

The new church in Thessalonica had a fear nobody had prepared them for. They were expecting Jesus to come back soon, maybe within their lifetimes. And then some of their own people died. A father. A friend. Had those who died missed it? Were they simply gone? You can hear the questions behind Paul's answer. It's one of the earliest Christian words to the grieving that we have, and Catholics still read it at funerals.
screen: `WAITING FOR HIS RETURN.` → `THEN SOME OF THEM DIED.` → `HAD THEY MISSED IT?`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And we will not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning them that are asleep, that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope." Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say don't grieve. He says don't grieve as those without hope. Grief stays. It's the hope that changes it. And notice the word he uses: asleep. Early Christians spoke of their dead that way, as sleeping until the resurrection. They called their burial grounds by a Greek word meaning sleeping places, and that word gives English cemetery. Then Paul gives the reason for the hope: if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have slept. The dead in Christ won't miss anything. In Paul's picture, they rise first, and the living meet them, and then: "so shall we be always with the Lord." And then the practical instruction: "Wherefore, comfort ye one another with these words." This passage isn't a timetable. It's comfort, meant to be said out loud to someone who's grieving. Catholics put it into practice in many ways. At a funeral, the coffin may be covered with a white pall, recalling the white garment of baptism, and the Easter candle stands beside it. In November the Church prays for the dead, especially on All Souls' Day. And the old Latin preface for funerals says it in four words: vita mutatur, non tollitur. Life is changed, not taken away. Christians grieve. They cry at gravesides like anyone. They just don't believe the grave is the end of the story.
screen: `NOT 'DON'T GRIEVE': GRIEVE WITH HOPE.` · `ASLEEP: THE SLEEPING PLACE.` · `ALWAYS WITH THE LORD.` · `COMFORT ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `NOT SORROWFUL, EVEN AS OTHERS WHO HAVE NO HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember one of your dead with hope. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've lost. If it's too fresh or too heavy today, choose someone further back, or simply someone the world has lost. Picture their face. Let yourself miss them. Don't hurry past it. Then remember one good thing about them, something you still carry. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, as Catholics do for their dead. If you don't, simply hold them, and say their name once, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Not as others without hope. Paul's words to grieving Thessalonians: Christians grieve, but with the hope of the resurrection. Today's word.
screen: `NOT AS OTHERS WITHOUT HOPE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: grieve with hope. Today, if someone you know is grieving, send them one line of comfort, not advice. Day five hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead, especially in November and on All Souls' Day (November 2), have Masses offered for them, and 1 Thessalonians 4 is among the readings for Catholic funerals.

fork.setup: your friends in Thessalonica are afraid their dead have missed Christ's return. you're Paul. what do you write?
options: tell them grief shows weak faith.
say the dead in Christ will rise, and comfort one another with these words.
say nobody can know anything about it.
fork.reveal: "that you be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope": the dead in Christ rise, and "so shall we be always with the Lord."

original.note: Greek: a sleeping place; early Christians used it for burial grounds, giving English 'cemetery'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Christians aren't supposed to be sad.
what it means: Christians grieve, but with hope in the resurrection, and comfort one another.
what a scholar hears: koimaomai, to sleep, and koimētērion, the cemetery; Douay-Rheims numbers this verse 4:12.

notes: Douay-Rheims verse numbering in 1 Thessalonians 4 runs one behind most Bibles (DR 4:12 = 4:13). Confirm numbering and wording.
Funeral rites: white pall and Paschal candle (Order of Christian Funerals). Confirm.
'Vita mutatur, non tollitur' from the Latin Preface I for the Dead; the English rendering is the script's own, not the ICEL text.
'Others who have no hope' is not applied to any present-day tradition in the voice.
